session_title: Architecture Decision: Managed Auth (Clerk/Auth0) vs In-House Custom OAuth2
objective: Determine whether to adopt a third-party managed identity platform or develop an internal OAuth2/OIDC microservice for our Q1 customer portal launch.

segments.speaker: Maya Lin (VP of Engineering)
segments.text: Welcome team. Our core agenda today is resolving the identity architecture for our customer launch. We have six weeks until private beta, and the board has made SOC2 Type II compliance mandatory before enterprise pilots can sign.

segments.speaker: David Kim (Product Manager)
segments.text: From product's vantage point, time to market is our paramount constraint. If we miss the Q1 beta window, three prospective enterprise pilots will churn to competitors. We need passwordless, passkeys, Google/Microsoft SSO, and SAML for enterprise tiers on day one.

segments.speaker: Carlos Gomez (Principal Architect)
segments.text: Technically, building our own OAuth2 server using FastAPI or Node is straightforward for basic username and password. However, when you factor in WebAuthn, FIDO2 passkeys, session revocation, rate-limiting brute-force vectors, and enterprise SAML integrations, we are looking at least three dedicated senior engineer sprints.

segments.speaker: Sarah Chen (Security & Compliance Lead)
segments.text: I want to highlight the compliance angle. An in-house authentication service requires penetration testing, third-party cryptographic code audits, and ongoing credential leak monitoring. With a SOC2 certified vendor like Clerk or Auth0, the shared responsibility model allows us to inherit 80% of identity-related security controls out of the box.

segments.speaker: Maya Lin (VP of Engineering)
segments.text: What about the cost trajectory? If our consumer volume spikes to 200,000 monthly active users, what is our monthly SaaS bill versus maintaining our own database instances and microservices?

segments.speaker: Carlos Gomez (Principal Architect)
segments.text: At 200k MAU, managed pricing ranges around $1,500 to $3,000 per month depending on feature tiers. That sounds like a lot, but one senior engineer's loaded cost is $22,000 a month. Even a quarter of an engineer's time spent on maintenance, token rotation, and vulnerability patches dwarfs the SaaS cost in years one and two.

segments.speaker: David Kim (Product Manager)
segments.text: And the opportunity cost is massive. Having Carlos and his team spend six weeks building auth means our core proprietary recommendation engine doesn't get built. Auth is a commodity expectation; our algorithms are our differentiator.

segments.speaker: Sarah Chen (Security & Compliance Lead)
segments.text: My recommendation is clear: adopt the managed identity provider immediately for our launch. To safeguard against vendor lock-in, we will design our internal backend with a provider-agnostic JWT verification layer and standard claims interface.

segments.speaker: Maya Lin (VP of Engineering)
segments.text: Consensus reached. We will proceed with the managed provider, wrap it behind a domain adapter, and allocate engineering capacity directly to customer-facing features. Thank you everyone.
